name: Learn: Multi-cluster Contexts
objective: CKA exam-environment skill: every task tells you which cluster to use via `kubectl config use-context`. Goal: work across TWO real clusters — create resources on the right one, never the wrong one, and always know your active context.
description: The #1 silly way to lose exam marks is running a correct command on the wrong cluster. This lab gives you two real clusters (kind-kindlab and kind-kindlab2) and makes you target each deliberately.

questions.title: Switch context and act on the right cluster
questions.teach:
A **context** is an entry in your kubeconfig that bundles three things: a **cluster** (API server URL + CA), a **user** (credentials), and a default **namespace**. The active context decides where every `kubectl` command lands.

**Inspecting / switching contexts:**
- `kubectl config get-contexts` — lists all contexts; the `*` marks the active one.
- `kubectl config current-context` — prints just the active context name.
- `kubectl config use-context <name>` — changes the *active* context (persists in kubeconfig).
- `kubectl config view` / `--minify` — shows the merged config (minify = only the active context).

**Three ways to target a specific cluster for a command:**
1. Switch first with `use-context`, then run normal commands (state persists across commands).
2. Per-command override: `kubectl --context <name> ...` (does NOT change the active context — safest for one-offs).
3. Point at an entirely different file: `kubectl --kubeconfig <file> ...` or the `KUBECONFIG` env var (colon-separated list merges multiple files).

**Set the default namespace of a context** so you stop typing `-n`: `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns>`.

**Exam gotchas:**
- The `*` in `get-contexts` is your truth source — glance at it before any create/delete.
- `--context` affects only that single command; it is easy to forget and then run the next command on the OLD active context.
- Context *name* vs cluster *name* vs user *name* are three separate fields; `kind` names contexts `kind-<clustername>`.
- `KUBECONFIG` as an env var overrides `~/.kube/config`; a stray export can make it look like resources vanished.

You have two clusters here: `kind-kindlab` (`$CTX`) and `kind-kindlab2` (`$CTX2`).
questions.prompt:
Switch to the **second** cluster and create a namespace `prod` **there** (on `$CTX2`), not on cluster1.

Target: namespace `prod` exists on cluster2 and does NOT exist on cluster1.
questions.hint: `kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab2` then `kubectl create namespace prod` — or in one shot: `kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 create ns prod`.
questions.solution:
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab2
kubectl create namespace prod
kubectl config get-contexts   # confirm the * is on kind-kindlab2

questions.title: Deploy onto cluster2
questions.teach: Once your active context is cluster2, normal commands (create, apply, delete, scale) all land there. Always glance at `kubectl config current-context` before a destructive or creative action. **Creating a Deployment imperatively:** - `kubectl create deployment --image= --replicas=` — fastest; add `-n ` for a namespace. - `--dry-run=client -o yaml` turns any imperative command into a YAML skeleton you can save, edit, and `apply -f` — the exam-friendly way to add fields `create deployment` can't set (resources, probes, volumes). - `kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml` — declarative; re-runnable and records the last-applied config. - `kubectl scale deployment --replicas=` — change replicas after creation. **Cross-cluster safety:** instead of (or before) switching, you can scope a single command with `kubectl --context $CTX2 -n prod create deployment ...` so there is no ambiguity about which cluster is hit. **Exam gotchas:** - `create deployment` does NOT accept `-l`/labels beyond its auto `app=`, and can set a port via `--port` but not env/resources/probes — reach for `--dry-run=client -o yaml` when you need more. - Omitting `-n` drops the resource into the context's default namespace (often `default`), not the one you meant. - A resource created on one cluster does NOT exist on the other — clusters are fully independent.
questions.prompt:
On cluster2, create a Deployment `api` (image `nginx:alpine`, 2 replicas) in the `prod` namespace.

Target: Deployment `api` with 2 replicas exists in `prod` on cluster2.
questions.solution: kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod create deployment api --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2

verification.description: Deployment 'api' (2 replicas) in prod on cluster2

questions.title: Now work on cluster1
questions.teach:
Switching back is just another `use-context`. The clusters are fully independent — a resource on one does not exist on the other.

**Creating a ConfigMap imperatively:**
- `--from-literal=key=value` — one or more inline key/value pairs (repeat the flag).
- `--from-file=<path>` — key is the filename, value is the file contents; `--from-file=key=<path>` renames the key.
- `--from-file=<dir>` — every file in the directory becomes a key.
- `--from-env-file=<file>` — each `KEY=VAL` line becomes a separate key.

**How workloads consume a ConfigMap (know all three):**
1. Single key as env var: `env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` (name + key).
2. Bulk env: `envFrom.configMapRef` injects every key as an env var.
3. Volume mount: mount the ConfigMap as a volume — each key becomes a file; use `subPath` to mount just one key as a single file.

Everything above is symmetric with **Secrets** (swap `configMap*` -> `secret*`, `configMapKeyRef` -> `secretKeyRef`, `configMapRef` -> `secretRef`).

**Exam gotchas:**
- `env`/`envFrom` are read ONCE at pod start — editing the ConfigMap won't update running pods; **mounted volumes** DO update (eventually). You must restart/roll pods for env changes.
- `immutable: true` locks a ConfigMap/Secret (only delete+recreate); good for performance, bad if you need edits.
- A missing key crashes the pod unless you mark it `optional: true`.
- Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted at rest by default; types include `Opaque`/generic, `kubernetes.io/tls`, `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson`.
questions.prompt:
Switch to **cluster1** (`$CTX`) and create a ConfigMap `shared-cfg` with key `env=prod` in the `default` namespace **there**.

Target: `shared-cfg` (env=prod) exists on cluster1 and NOT on cluster2.
questions.hint: `kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab` then `kubectl create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod`.
questions.solution:
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab
kubectl create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod

questions.title: Replicate a resource across clusters
questions.teach:
A common exam/real task: take something from one cluster to another. Two approaches:

**Recreate imperatively** on the target (cleanest when the resource is simple):
`kubectl --context $CTX2 -n prod create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod`.

**Pipe YAML across** (preserves everything):
`kubectl --context $CTX -n <ns> get cm shared-cfg -o yaml | kubectl --context $CTX2 -n prod create -f -`.

**Scrub server-populated fields before re-creating** — a raw `get -o yaml` carries cluster-specific metadata that will reject or mislead on the target:
- `metadata.namespace` (set the new one via `-n`),
- `metadata.uid`, `resourceVersion`, `creationTimestamp`, `generation`,
- the whole `status:` block.
Use `--export` is GONE (removed); instead pipe through a cleanup, or just `kubectl get ... -o yaml | kubectl neat` if available, or hand-edit.

**Exam gotchas:**
- Change the target namespace with `-n` on the second command; the embedded `namespace:` field, if present and different, wins over `-n` — strip it to avoid surprises.
- `create -f -` fails if the object already exists; `apply -f -` is idempotent (upsert).
- The `--context` on EACH side of the pipe is independent — forgetting one sends you back to the active context.
- Secrets copied this way keep their base64 `data:` values verbatim, which is fine; just confirm the `type:` field survives.
questions.prompt:
Replicate `shared-cfg` (env=prod) into the `prod` namespace on **cluster2**.

Target: ConfigMap `shared-cfg` with `env=prod` exists in `prod` on cluster2.
questions.hint: Simplest: `kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod`.
questions.solution: kubectl --context kind-kindlab2 -n prod create configmap shared-cfg --from-literal=env=prod

verification.description: shared-cfg (env=prod) exists in prod on cluster2

questions.title: Context discipline — know where you are
questions.teach:
The single habit that saves the most marks on a multi-cluster exam: after finishing on one cluster, set your active context to where the *next* task expects, and verify. Never assume.

**Verify your position (cheap, do it often):**
- `kubectl config current-context` — the active context name.
- `kubectl config get-contexts` — the `*` column confirms it visually.
- `kubectl config view --minify` — shows the cluster server URL + namespace actually in play.

**Fast context operations worth memorising:**
- `kubectl config use-context <name>` — switch active context.
- `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns>` — change default namespace without retyping `-n`.
- `kubectl config rename-context <old> <new>` / `delete-context <name>` — housekeeping.
- Per-command `--context <name>` leaves the active context untouched — use it so you never *leave* the wrong cluster selected.

**Exam gotchas:**
- Many tasks say "on cluster X" — if you leave the active context on the wrong cluster, a *correct* command silently grades as wrong. Switch, verify, then act.
- `use-context` persists to the kubeconfig file, so your choice survives into the next task's shell.
- Setting a default namespace with `set-context` is per-CONTEXT; switching contexts resets you to that context's own default namespace.
- If `KUBECONFIG` points at a merged list, `use-context` writes to the FIRST writable file — confirm with `config view` if things look off.
questions.prompt:
Leave your **active** context set to cluster1 (`$CTX`).

Target: `kubectl config current-context` returns `kind-kindlab`.
questions.solution:
kubectl config use-context kind-kindlab
kubectl config current-context   # kind-kindlab
